title: Trump says Iran war could end after U.S. elections as Hormuz tensions persist
full_text:
U.S. stocks end higher as Fed hike bets wane, but post weekly loss on bond rout
Investing.com -- U.S. President Donald Trump said the war with Iran could end "very soon, probably right after the elections," as fighting intensified in Yemen and attacks on shipping continued around the Strait of Hormuz.
Speaking at a rally in Alabama, Trump reiterated that Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon and questioned who Washington could negotiate with in Tehran. He also highlighted the U.S. blockade and said oil prices would fall once the conflict ended. He offered no details on how an agreement might be reached.
His comments came as diplomatic efforts remained stalled. Iran has been awaiting a definitive U.S. response to its proposal for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran previously saying it would not soften its conditions.
Tensions around the waterway remained elevated. A crude oil tanker was struck by an unknown projectile off Oman, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency. All crew members were reported safe, and authorities were investigating.
Separately, the IRGC said Iranian forces had "full control" of the Strait of Hormuz, according to the Iraqi News Agency.
The energy fallout prompted G7 countries to agree to release up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude reserves over four months. International Energy Agency chief Fatih Birol said oil prices had begun falling following the decision. Trump subsequently said Washington would not proceed with a threatened export ban.
The conflict also continued spreading through Yemen. The internationally recognised government’s armed forces said they conducted 474 attacks against Houthi positions over 24 hours, killing or wounding 1,540 fighters. The Houthis have not confirmed those casualty figures.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence said debris from an intercepted ballistic missile injured a resident in the southern Asir region. A separate Houthi projectile struck a school in Najran, causing damage but no reported casualties.
The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted three ballistic missiles targeting Khamis Mushait. The Houthis separately accused Saudi forces of carrying out dozens of strikes across Yemen.
Washington also increased economic pressure on Tehran, joining 66 countries in calling for enforcement of reimposed UN sanctions and urging Iran to return to its international non-proliferation commitments.

title: Bitcoin holds below $85,000 as SEC custody proposal boosts institutional outlook
full_text:
U.S. stocks end higher as Fed hike bets wane, but post weekly loss on bond rout
Investing.com -- Bitcoin held below $85,000 on Friday after briefly topping $87,000, with a new U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission proposal on crypto custody adding to expectations of broader institutional participation.
Bitcoin was trading at $84,612.4 as of 21:55 ET (01:55 GMT), down 0.35% after reaching an intraday high of $87,219, its first move above $87,000 since Sept. 23. The cryptocurrency remained higher on the day after spending much of the previous session around $84,500 to $85,000.
The SEC proposed changes to custody rules that would allow investment advisers and funds to directly hold certain digital assets when a qualified third-party custodian is unavailable, subject to safeguards.
Existing frameworks have largely relied on traditional custodians, creating difficulties for advisers seeking exposure to assets for which qualified custody services are limited. The SEC proposal would provide another route for funds and advisers to hold such assets under federal securities rules.
The proposal will enter a 60-day public comment period following publication in the Federal Register.
Bitcoin also received some support from softer U.S. economic data. September nonfarm payrolls rose 29,000, below expectations of 90,000, prompting declines in Treasury yields and the dollar as markets reassessed the outlook for Federal Reserve interest rates.
The price increase triggered substantial liquidations among traders positioned for a decline. About $142 million of Bitcoin short positions were liquidated over 24 hours, compared with roughly $29 million in long positions, according to Coinglass data cited in the source material.
Corporate demand remains another part of the Bitcoin market. Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) Executive Chairman Michael Saylor this week detailed how the company finances its Bitcoin-focused business and maintains dollar reserves for dividends and debt interest.
Strategy’s model separates Bitcoin accumulation from cash required to meet obligations. Its STRC preferred shares currently carry a 12% annualized dividend rate, and the company proposes switching to daily dividend accruals, which shareholders are scheduled to vote on Oct. 28.
A newer entrant is taking a different approach. Supercycle Finance said it plans to raise up to $75 million through a proposed offering, with most of the proceeds intended for Bitcoin purchases. Unlike accumulation-focused treasury companies, it plans to sell Bitcoin during periods it considers elevated and hold interest-bearing assets between purchases.

title: Why rising exports aren’t easing oil market fears
full_text:
U.S. stocks end higher as Fed hike bets wane, but post weekly loss on bond rout
Investing.com -- Middle East oil exports are recovering toward pre-war levels, but soaring freight costs, tanker shortages and disruption around key shipping routes are keeping pressure on the market, according to PVM Oil Associates, part of TP ICAP Group.
Middle East exports reached an estimated 80% of pre-war levels, with shipments averaging about 12.8 million barrels per day in September. Saudi exports climbed to roughly 6 million barrels per day, approaching their 2025 monthly average.
Iraq’s production also rose to 3.5 million barrels per day in August as exports through southern terminals improved.
Much of the recovery relies on more complex shipping arrangements. Ship-to-ship transfers have become a key workaround, with tankers loading inside the Gulf before transferring cargo off Sohar in Oman or Fujairah in the UAE, outside the Strait of Hormuz.
Around 2.5 million barrels per day were expected to move through such transfers in September, up from 1.4 million in August.
These two-stage journeys require more vessels and expose operators to higher insurance and chartering costs. The International Maritime Organization has verified 80 attacks on merchant vessels around Hormuz since the conflict began on Feb. 28, resulting in at least 22 seafarer deaths.
Tanker availability has tightened sharply. Daily charter rates for very large crude carriers originating inside the Gulf and transiting Hormuz have reached records of between $1 million and $1.27 million, according to LSEG data cited in the report.
Pressure is also spreading beyond oil. Spot container rates between the Far East and northern Europe have risen 85% since the Iran war began, reaching an average of $4,100.
Floating oil storage is shrinking as vessels become more valuable for transporting cargo. Global floating storage fell from 145 million barrels in April to around 88 million.
Recovering exports have therefore done little to remove concerns over limited shipping capacity and elevated transport costs, leaving freight as a major source of pressure across oil markets.

title: US appeals court blocks Minnesota law barring ’nudified’ photos in XAI lawsuit
full_text:
U.S. stocks end higher as Fed hike bets wane, but post weekly loss on bond rout
WASHINGTON, Oct 2 (Reuters) - Elon Musk’s xAI on Friday persuaded a US federal appeals court to halt Minnesota’s first-in-the-nation ban on AI-generated fake nude images as the technology and social media company pursues a lawsuit alleging that the law is unconstitutional.
The St. Louis-based 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals in its order put the law on hold for now, granting a request for an injunction by xAI. A lower court judge last month had rejected Musk’s bid for an order stopping the law.
The state’s anti-"nudification" law, which took effect on August 1, prohibits website operators, software developers and others from allowing users to create realistic images depicting an intimate body part that is not shown in an original photo of an identifiable individual.
xAI alleges the measure restricts free speech protected by the US Constitution.
Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison’s office said in a statement on Friday it is disappointed by the appeals court ruling and will defend the new state law as xAI’s appeal moves forward.
"Minnesota’s nudification ban outlaws AI technology products from generating sexual images that harm and harass people in the vilest way possible," Ellison spokesperson John Stiles said.
xAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
US District Judge Donovan Frank ruled last month that xAI had not shown it would suffer irreparable harm while challenging the law and said the company had waited too long to seek emergency relief.
In its appeal, xAI disputed the judge’s finding that it delayed bringing suit. The company also said its Grok Imagine tool includes "rigorous protections" against creating nudified or sexualized images of real people.
xAI has begun suing users whom it alleges are evading Grok’s technological blockers to create sexual images of people without their consent.
Minnesota had urged the appeals court not to block the law. The state has said it adopted the measure this year to combat the spread of what it called a "staggering amount (of) child sexual abuse material that AI products like Grok Imagine generate."

title: Xi’s rest breaks cut hours from Trump summit schedule - WSJ
full_text:
U.S. stocks end higher as Fed hike bets wane, but post weekly loss on bond rout
Investing.com -- Chinese officials sought unusually long rest periods for President Xi Jinping during his recent Washington summit with U.S. President Donald Trump, cutting hours from the leaders’ schedule, the Wall Street Journal reported exclusively.
Beijing’s requests included a private room inside the West Wing where Xi could rest between events, with only his wife, Peng Liyuan, permitted to join him, according to people familiar with planning for the visit.
Chinese officials also declined a planned working lunch between Xi and Trump on Sept. 24, the summit’s only full day, saying they preferred additional downtime for Xi. The scheduling changes resulted in a roughly five-hour gap in the agenda during a visit lasting less than two days.
No activities were arranged for Xi on the evening of his arrival following a roughly 14-hour flight from Beijing. His visit to the National Archives on Sept. 25 lasted about 10 minutes, shorter than U.S. officials had planned.
The Journal said Xi’s team also structured the schedule around considerations including how long he could stand and walk and when he would need breaks. Dennis Wilder, a former senior China director at the National Security Council, described the private room arrangement as unusual compared with previous state visits he helped organize.
The bilateral meeting at the White House on Sept. 24 began close to noon and ended by early afternoon. Xi then left the White House and returned for the state dinner that evening, limiting the time available for substantive discussions.
The report pointed to visible caution in Xi’s movements during the visit, including holding Peng’s hand as he descended aircraft stairs and climbed steps at the National Archives.
The Journal said some scheduling changes could be explained by jet lag. It also cited analysts who said they saw no signs of cognitive decline in Xi’s public appearances.
Questions surrounding China’s leadership succession have attracted attention because Xi has not designated a successor. He holds China’s three major leadership positions as Communist Party general secretary, president, and chairman of the Central Military Commission.

title: Japan shifts messaging to counter view its policies are reflationary, Katayama says in TV interview
full_text:
TOKYO, Oct 3 (Reuters) - Japan’s government has begun recalibrating its messaging to reassure markets that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is not pursuing reflationary policies, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said in an interview with broadcaster TV Tokyo on Saturday.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent views Takaichi’s economic policies as suited to current economic conditions, but has questioned whether the government has been communicating that message clearly enough to investors, Katayama said.
"So we concluded around late August that we need to communicate that message more clearly to financial markets," Katayama said, addressing market perceptions that the administration’s policies are reflationary.

title: How big can Starlink’s residential broadband business become?
full_text:
U.S. stocks end higher as Fed hike bets wane, but post weekly loss on bond rout
Investing.com -- SpaceX’s Starlink could reach roughly 150 million residential broadband subscribers and generate up to $65 billion in annual subscription revenue, Bernstein analysts said.
Starlink had about 12 million total subscribers as of the second quarter of 2026, up from virtually none in 2020. That figure includes residential customers alongside roaming users, small businesses and other applications.
The service is available in more than 120 countries and territories, with another 50-plus markets listed as coming soon. Bernstein estimates more than 800 million residential broadband subscriptions exist across markets Starlink currently serves or could eventually enter.
Legacy satellite broadband represents the most immediate opportunity, but the market is relatively small. Capturing the existing satellite and other fixed-broadband base would produce about 13 million residential subscribers and $4 billion to $7 billion in annual subscription revenue.
A bigger opportunity comes from households without fixed broadband. Roughly half of occupied households globally remain unconnected, although affordability could limit adoption. Adding selected unconnected households could lift Starlink to 50 million to 75 million residential subscribers and $12 billion to $21 billion in revenue.
The analysts see the more plausible scenario as Starlink also capturing 10% to 20% of non-fibre broadband customers, including DSL, fixed wireless and selected cable users. That could produce roughly 93 million to 153 million residential subscribers and $27 billion to $65 billion in annual subscription revenue.
Taking meaningful fibre market share could lift the opportunity toward 200 million subscribers and $90 billion in revenue, though the analysts view that scenario as less likely given fibre’s superior performance.
Including small businesses and other consumer broadband uses, the 2031 base case reaches about 168 million subscribers and $64 billion in annual revenue. Subscriber growth is expected to come with declining average revenue per user as Starlink expands into lower-income markets and adopts more competitive local pricing.

title: Consumer AI agents: What does it mean for Financial Services?
full_text:
U.S. stocks end higher as Fed hike bets wane, but post weekly loss on bond rout
Investing.com -- Consumer AI agents could challenge long-standing sources of friction across financial services, but trust, data access, and regulation remain major barriers to widespread adoption, Bernstein analysts said.
The debate has intensified following the rapid adoption of Meta’s Muse, which reached 2.8 million downloads and became the top-ranked app in the U.S. App Store. Financial stocks exposed to consumer inertia have reacted negatively, with mortgage lenders, brokers, regional banks and insurers falling between 6% and 14% since Muse launched.
AI agents could automatically compare insurance policies, move deposits, optimize broker cash balances and select between credit-card rewards and offers. Such capabilities could weaken customer stickiness and pressure revenue from deposits, cash sweeps, insurance renewals and financial advice.
Yet adoption is not simply a question of whether AI can perform those tasks. Consumers must be willing to delegate financial decisions, and providers must permit agents to access accounts, pricing and other data.
Financial institutions also retain control over authentication, identity checks, account access and product eligibility. Banks could potentially charge AI agents for data access, mirroring JPMorgan’s decision to charge data aggregators.
Trust presents another obstacle. A TD Bank survey found 55% of Americans use AI to help manage their finances, up from 10% a year earlier, but only 18% were comfortable allowing AI to independently make important financial decisions.
Liability and regulation add further complications, including questions around consumer consent, financial advice, licensing and responsibility when an agent makes an unsuitable decision.
Payments could be better positioned than other financial sectors. Visa and Mastercard’s existing fraud protections, dispute systems and tokenized credentials could become more valuable as agent-driven transactions increase.
Payment processors may also benefit from helping merchants manage multiple AI platforms and protocols, with Adyen already launching tools designed to connect enterprises with AI-driven commerce.
The transition is expected to take time, with trust, data access and regulation likely determining how deeply consumer AI agents reshape financial services.

title: FlyDubai attacker used crash ax in cockpit attack, UAE says - WSJ
full_text:
U.S. stocks end higher as Fed hike bets wane, but post weekly loss on bond rout
Investing.com -- The co-pilot accused of attacking the captain of a FlyDubai flight to Israel used an onboard crash ax in an attempt to seize control of the aircraft, the United Arab Emirates said Saturday, according to the Wall Street Journal.
UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said the co-pilot began carrying out his plan during Wednesday’s Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, attacking the captain inside the flight deck with the ax and attempting to take control of the flight controls.
The disclosure indicates the attacker likely did not need to smuggle a weapon onto the aircraft. Crash axes are carried on commercial aircraft for emergencies such as fighting fires or cutting through metal, and UAE aviation regulations require one to be stored onboard.
Al Shamsi said authorities were continuing to investigate the circumstances and motive behind the attack, including any possible links, and were examining physical and digital evidence.
The WSJ previously identified the co-pilot as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national who had been banned from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views.
It remains unclear whether Omani authorities communicated those concerns to FlyDubai or UAE officials before the incident.
The captain was injured during the attack, and the aircraft came close to crashing before passengers and crew members overpowered Hammami, according to the Journal’s earlier reporting. The flight subsequently made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
UAE authorities are investigating the incident, which officials have described as an act of terrorism. FlyDubai suspended its Dubai-Tel Aviv service following the attack.
The earlier WSJ report said Hammami’s previous ban in Oman had raised questions about aviation security procedures and the sharing of information between authorities.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and a UAE presidential adviser characterized the attack as terrorism, according to the Journal.

title: G20 countries split over U.S. push to curb excess industrial capacity
full_text:
U.S. stocks end higher as Fed hike bets wane, but post weekly loss on bond rout
Investing.com -- A "handful" of the Group of 20 trade ministers rejected a U.S.-led push to address excess industrial capacity and non-market economic policies, exposing divisions among major economies, Reuters reported.
The U.S. Trade Representative’s office said a draft ministerial statement on excess capacity was supported by most G20 members, but several countries firmly rejected creating a framework for cooperative action.
Washington, which holds this year’s G20 presidency, did not identify the countries that opposed the proposal. China previously objected to a similar statement targeting forced labour and non-market economic policies at a G20 finance meeting last month.
Beijing has rejected U.S. accusations that its industrial subsidies and policies have generated excess capacity, arguing that Western countries are using the issue to justify protectionist measures.
The dispute comes as USTR conducts a Section 301 investigation into 16 trading partners showing signs of excess industrial capacity, a process expected to potentially result in additional tariffs in coming months.
Separately, only Mexico and Argentina backed a U.S.-led statement seeking greater cooperation to remove goods produced with forced labour from global supply chains.
The Trump administration has imposed tariffs of 10% or 12.5% on goods from 59 countries and the European Union, alleging inadequate enforcement of forced-labour restrictions.
G20 trade ministers did reach consensus on condemning the use of food trade for economic or political coercion. Members agreed that measures designed to restrict or redirect food and agricultural inputs to extract unrelated geopolitical concessions posed humanitarian and economic risks.
Trade ministers also discussed potential changes to the World Trade Organization’s most-favoured-nation tariff system.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has argued that the system limits countries’ ability to respond differently to economies using non-market policies. The U.S. said some G20 members were open to considering expanded exceptions or new legal interpretations of existing rules.

title: Pressure builds on Iran as Trump expands U.S. military presence - Bloomberg
full_text:
U.S. stocks end higher as Fed hike bets wane, but post weekly loss on bond rout
Investing.com -- Iran is facing mounting economic and military pressure as the U.S. expands its presence in the Middle East and regional oil exports recover, Bloomberg reported exclusively, citing officials and analysts.
President Donald Trump’s administration is sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt and about 10,000 additional sailors and Marines toward the region. Its arrival could give the U.S. three carrier strike groups in the Middle East, though one of the existing carriers could depart.
Iran’s economy is also under growing strain. Inflation is approaching 90%, and the rial has lost about 25% against the dollar over the past two months and almost half its value this year.
A U.S. blockade has sharply reduced Iran’s crude exports. Preliminary estimates showed the country loaded no crude onto tankers in September, though some Chinese refiners continue receiving oil from floating storage.
Tehran has redirected more trade through land borders and the Caspian Sea, but those routes lack the capacity to fully replace Persian Gulf shipments.
At the same time, Iran’s ability to restrict regional energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz appears to be under pressure. Saudi crude exports climbed to about 6.1 million barrels per day in September from 3.4 million in August.
JPMorgan estimates Middle East crude shipments have recovered to 17.5 million barrels per day, equivalent to 98% of pre-war levels.
Officials offered conflicting assessments of Iran’s control over Hormuz, with one regional defence official saying Tehran retains substantial influence and another saying its grip is weakening.
Diplomatic efforts remain deadlocked. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has suggested restoring access for nuclear inspectors in exchange for sanctions relief, according to diplomats cited by Bloomberg.
Washington has also expanded economic pressure, imposing sanctions on major Iranian automakers and rail companies on Oct. 1 after earlier measures disrupted Iranian aviation links.
Iran, meanwhile, is preparing for the possibility of renewed U.S. bombing, according to an Iranian official. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has warned it would respond to any new U.S. or Israeli attack.

title: Analysis-AI’s race to transform the world before the money runs out
full_text:
U.S. stocks end higher as Fed hike bets wane, but post weekly loss on bond rout
By Stephen Eisenhammer
LONDON, Oct 3 (Reuters) - Never has so much cash flowed into a new technology as is pouring into AI, eclipsing the sums splurged on railways or the internet when those technological revolutions sucked in capital.
Cumulative spending globally on data centers alone could top $30 trillion by 2050, according to a projection by PwC, almost matching the value of outstanding US Treasuries. It "dwarfs" what was spent in the railroad or dotcom booms, even after adjusting for inflation, PwC said.
Meanwhile, Anthropic, just one of the major firms in the AI race, plans to spend $518 billion in coming years, according to the IPO prospectus seen by Reuters, which is more than 100 times its 2025 revenue. Its backers say AI technology will be more transformational than the advent of steam engines and the industrialization they powered.
Yet lurking behind the dizzying projections and huge outlays by AI companies, alongside sky-high valuations, lie assumptions about vast broad-based productivity gains and future profits with little evidence so far - or historical precedent - to be sure they can deliver, economists say.
PRODUCTIVITY GAINS ’REMAIN ELUSIVE’
JP Morgan wrote in August that broad-based productivity gains in the US, which leads the AI race, "remain elusive", raising questions about the sustainability of AI valuations.
A Bain & Company study said productivity gains from existing markets would not be enough to justify current outlays and "entirely new markets must emerge to close the funding gap", suggesting those could range from using AI-guided robots to developing new materials for batteries and semiconductors.
US hyperscalers - the companies rolling out infrastructure around the world like Google, Amazon and Microsoft - and others in the AI race needed to find more than $4.2 trillion of new revenue in the next five years to fund the buildout, Bain said.
"The question is whether the applications arrive in time to pay for it," according to the study, published last month.
Few doubt the potential of AI to transform everything from work in an office to research labs, just as past revolutions shrank journey times from days to hours or connected the world at the touch of a keyboard.
What seems more immutable is the maths behind securing a return on investment or the deadlines for repaying loans, leaving economists to work out the implications for the global economy beyond the ups and downs of investment cycles.
"Historical precedent suggests that technology-driven booms often end when infrastructure buildouts cease to deliver sufficient returns," JP Morgan wrote.
Using the example of Nvidia, the US company whose chips are the backbone of the AI revolution, JP Morgan estimated US productivity gains would need to be 3% to 5% annually over the next 10 years to justify its valuation. That would be a substantial increase from the baseline expectation of the US Congressional Budget Office of 1.75% annual productivity growth for that period.
For the US alone - which according to some estimates accounts for about three quarters of the global AI investment total - investment will run as high as about $9 trillion from 2025 to 2032, equivalent to spending 3.2% of US GDP each year, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh.
He estimates the US AI sector would need to generate about $3.55 trillion in annual revenue by 2032 to earn a 10% return on investment. It earns a fraction of that now.
The leveraged structure of much of the debt funding AI infrastructure also means "a relatively modest deterioration in demand, delays, or asset values can therefore produce much larger losses," he wrote in a conference paper, revised in October.
AI AND ’THE RATE OF NEW WONDERS’
The dizzying numbers have not stopped US AI bosses speaking with an otherworldly zeal about changes afoot.
Anthropic’s Dario Amodei has said an AI future could be "a thing of transcendent beauty", while OpenAI’s Sam Altman has said "the rate of new wonders being achieved will be immense" as models learn to improve themselves and accelerate breakthroughs.
Jasjeet Sekhon, chief strategy officer at Google DeepMind, told a summit at UC Berkeley in August that this self-teaching, known as recursive self-improvement, was a "key part of the investment thesis", and that it could, if achieved, deliver unprecedented productivity gains.
Recursive self-improvement, while potentially delivering exponential AI advances, has also raised concerns about existential risks to humanity.
Yet the pace of change in productivity might still end up lagging the timelines needed by corporate accounts departments.
Diane Coyle, an economist at Britain’s Cambridge University, said the productivity impact of past revolutionary technologies had usually taken about 10 to 50 years to feed through.
Anthropic’s economics team modeled a range of scenarios for how much extra growth AI would deliver at an annual rate in 2030. Assuming a baseline of 2% in a non-AI environment, it suggested growth of 2.4% in a scenario with modest AI impact, 5.4% in a substantial scenario and 15.4% in an extreme scenario.
Higher growth would mean more jobs lost, it said, without assigning probabilities for any of the outcomes.
Amodei forecast last year that AI could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within five years. For now, however, some researchers say it appears to have been limited to making it harder for those seeking office work to find a job.
Studies in the US and Britain have pointed to a slowdown in early career hiring for white-collar positions performing tasks at which AI is adept, even if overall employment remains strong.
Researchers at Stanford University said in August that employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed industries, such as accountants and paralegals, was 19% lower than for jobs that AI found hard to replicate, like janitors and builders.
Yet even if the promised transformation takes longer than numbers surrounding AI companies imply, real economic benefits should stay - just as trains still ran after the Panic of 1873 that bankrupted railroad barons, while the internet didn’t shut down after the 1990s dotcom bubble burst.
"History is our friend in trying to understand this," said Coyle. "As long as one is left with the infrastructure that’s needed to support all the productivity effects down the road, that’s okay."

title: Flydubai co-pilot attacked pilot with axe, attempted ’terrorist’ attack, UAE says
full_text:
U.S. stocks end higher as Fed hike bets wane, but post weekly loss on bond rout
Oct 3 (Reuters) - The co-pilot of flydubai flight FZ1073 attempted to carry out a "terrorist" attack during the flight, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said on Saturday, according to the state news agency WAM.
The co-pilot was identified as Hammam al-Hammami, an Omani national, a source with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters. UAE authorities did not immediately respond to a request for confirmation of his identity.
The co-pilot attacked the pilot inside the cockpit with a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft, the prosecutor general said.
A crash axe is typically kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies such as crashes.
Investigations are ongoing to determine the circumstances of the incident, the motives and any related connections, as well as to examine physical and digital evidence, he added.
UAE Prosecutor General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi’s comments were the first by Emirati authorities to describe the incident as an attempted "terrorist" attack.
Disaster was averted on Wednesday after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had attacked the captain in what Israeli officials said was an apparent attempt to crash the plane carrying more than 170 passengers and crew.
A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.
Flydubai said the circumstances surrounding the incident were still under investigation and that it was not in a position to comment further, a spokesperson said.
An Israeli government official told Reuters earlier that Israeli investigators would take part alongside Emirati authorities in the UAE-led investigation, which would examine what happened as well as the suspect’s motives and background.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday that Israel was looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone’s direction, warning that anyone involved would pay a "heavy price".
Netanyahu said on Thursday that the co-pilot, whom he identified as an Omani national, had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and appeared suicidal, though he said a motive had not yet been established. Most of the passengers on board were Israeli nationals.
The aircraft dropped about 16,625 feet in just over 30 seconds while flying over Saudi Arabia on its journey from the UAE to Israel, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24. The route is popular among Israeli travellers.
